_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: It differs from a camel: in that it resembles its mother in some of its signs.
rashi:a2.1: Is forbidden for consumption: and whom have you heard holding this view? Rabbi Shimon. [It then teaches:] “And if its head and the majority of its body…” And it was assumed that since it teaches the two together, learn from it that even for consumption Rabbi Shimon requires its head and the majority of its body.
tosafot:a2.1: Learn from it that for consumption too Rabbi Shimon requires its head and the majority of its body: for it implies that there are only two categories [in the baraita], since it does not teach a third category, saying: If it has some of the signs it is permitted for consumption, and then teach: And if its head and the majority of its body resemble its mother it is obligated in firstborn status. As it stands, both the first clause and the latter clause teach a novelty: the first clause teaches that [a kosher animal] gave birth to a non-kosher kind, which is forbidden even for consumption, and the latter clause teaches that if its head and the majority of its body resemble its mother, it is obligated even in firstborn status.
rashi:a3.1: Since it leaves consumption: which it discussed in the first clause, and turns to firstborn status, and does not say: If its head and the majority of its body resemble its mother it is permitted for consumption, learn from it that for consumption some of the signs suffice.
rashi:a4.1: It was necessary for firstborn status: but actually, for both we require its head and the majority of its body.
rashi:a5.1: These you may not eat: a camel, even if it was born from a cow.
rashi:a5.2: But you may eat another that comes with one sign: of its mother; that is, one that resembles its mother in part, such as a non-kosher animal born from a kosher one that resembles its mother in part.
tosafot:a5.1: These you may not eat: the camel and the hyrax are written in the verse. “But you may eat what comes with one sign” does not speak of the signs of kosher status, chewing the cud and having split hooves, but of resembling its mother in some features: in the forelegs, in the hind legs and in its wool. [To be kosher by its own] signs of kosher status, it requires [both of] the signs.
rashi:a7.1: Seh kesavim: a seh [lamb] that comes from two sheep.
tosafot:a7.1: Unless its father and its mother are sheep: Rabbi Yehoshua expounds this from the fact that it is written kesavim and izzim [in the plural], and not keves and ez, and Rabbi Eliezer from the fact that seh, seh is written twice. So the exposition Rabbi Yehoshua uses to forbid is not the one Rabbi Eliezer uses to permit. The phrase “the verse does not come,” which Rabbi Eliezer says, is somewhat awkward, for the wording implies that this very verse, which Rabbi Yehoshua expounded about a non-kosher animal born from a kosher one whose conception was from a kosher one, Rabbi Eliezer says comes to add to the permitted, permitting a non-kosher animal born from a kosher one whose conception was from a non-kosher one. One may explain “the verse does not come” like “the Torah did not come” [a general expression]. Alternatively, one may say this is the meaning of Rabbi Eliezer’s words: from “seh, seh” we derive [the case where] its conception was from a kosher animal; therefore “these” is left over to add to the permitted, [even where] its conception was from a non-kosher animal.
rashi:a8.1: To permit the permitted: since its father and mother are kosher, this verse, “Yet these you may eat,” was not needed to permit it.
rashi:a8.2: In any case: since seh is written twice, learn from it that [it is permitted] even [if it is a sheep] on its mother’s side and not on its father’s side.
rashi:a9.1: He calls it non-kosher: the animal with closed hooves [kalut] that was born from a kosher one.
rashi:a9.2: In accordance with Rabbi Shimon: who forbids it where it does not have some of the signs; and he says that if it has one sign of kosher status, resembling its mother in part, it is permitted.
rashi:a10.1: And disagrees with him on one: for Rabbi Shimon requires its head and the majority of its body.
rashi:a11.1: And there are those who raise a difficulty: a difficulty against this baraita, and from within the difficulty one answers the questioner [on the dilemma] whether Rabbi Shimon requires its head and the majority of its body for consumption or not.
rashi:a11.2: Does it become pregnant: [can] a kosher animal [become pregnant] from a non-kosher one, as it teaches, “and its conception was from a non-kosher animal”?
rashi:a13.1: Except for Rabbi Eliezer and his disputants: who disagree about the koy in chapter Oto Ve’et Beno in Sheḥitat Ḥullin (79b), whether [the prohibition of slaughtering] it and its offspring [on one day] applies to it; and it teaches there that a koy comes from a he-goat and a female gazelle. Evidently, according to them, an undomesticated animal becomes pregnant from a domesticated one.
tosafot:a13.1: Except for Rabbi Eliezer and his disputants: that he does not say “except for the dulfanin, which reproduce from people,” as is said below [8a], is no difficulty at all, for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi speaks only of domesticated and undomesticated animals, not of people, and those are creatures of the sea.
rashi:a14.1: And Rabbi Yirmeya says: this “its conception was from a non-kosher animal” that it says means that it became pregnant from a kalut, whose hooves are closed like a camel’s, and which is the offspring of a cow. In accordance with Rabbi Shimon he calls it non-kosher, and its offspring is permitted if it resembles its mother in one sign. Evidently, for consumption Rabbi Shimon does not require its head and the majority of its body.
tosafot:a15.1: And disagrees with him on one: what it can deflect, it deflects in this way, because in the conclusion we resolve that for consumption too Rabbi Shimon requires its head and the majority of its body.
rashi:a16.1: This and that cause: the permitted and the forbidden [parent together] cause this one to come about, it being non-kosher and its mother kosher.
rashi:a17.1: The offspring of a tereifa: and its father is unblemished; this is “this and that cause.”
tosafot:a17.1: But we have heard them say the opposite, the offspring of a tereifa: according to the one who says a tereifa can give birth, it is well: they disagree about “this and that cause.” But according to the one who says it cannot give birth, the dispute is set, in chapter Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 58a), where [the principle] “a fetus is its mother’s thigh” [applies], and it became pregnant and afterward became a tereifa. Yet we find elsewhere that Rabbi Eliezer holds “this and that cause” is forbidden and the Rabbis hold it is permitted: regarding leaven of non-sacred produce and of teruma, and at the end of Kol HaTzelamim (Avoda Zara 49a), regarding one who took wood from it [an ashera]. Rather, it is brought [here] for Rabbi Yehoshua, even though it is not everyone’s view. As for its speaking of “this and that cause” here, while in chapter Oto Ve’et Beno (Ḥullin 79b) it uses the expression “one is concerned about the seed of the father”: here it speaks of something that comes from the permitted and the forbidden, [so] “this and that cause” fits well. It is difficult, though: since one is not concerned about the seed of the father, for what reason should the offspring of a tereifa count as “this and that cause”? Let [the father] not count, so that the leaven [the forbidden element alone] causes it, and let it be forbidden.
rashi:a18.1: For if so: that [an offspring whose] conception was from a non-kosher animal is forbidden, let it write “seh kesavim ve’izzim.”
rashi:a23.1: Water enters, water exits, and that it is turbid is the heat of the flesh: due to the warmth and the putrefaction of the flesh.
rashi:a24.1: Mittamei would imply from the body of the non-kosher animal; min hattamei implies of the kind [min] of the non-kosher, that is, these, which resemble milk.
gershom:a1.1: Come and hear: a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher kind is forbidden for consumption. This baraita is Rabbi Shimon’s, for he is the one who says it is forbidden for consumption; and it teaches: if its head and the majority of its body resemble its mother it is obligated in firstborn status. Learn from it that the same is true for consumption: Rabbi Shimon requires its head and the majority of its body, not only for firstborn status.
gershom:a2.1: These you may not eat, the camel, etc., but you may eat what comes with one sign: that is, if it has some partial resemblance.
gershom:a3.1: The verse states: “Seh kesavim and seh izzim.” It extends [the requirement]: until its father is a ram and its mother a ewe.
gershom:a4.1: The verse does not come to permit the permitted: where its father too is a ram; rather, to add to the permitted. And which is this? “These you may eat.”
gershom:a5.1: Or perhaps not: that the verse is needed only [where] its conception was from a kosher animal, and that “to add to the permitted” means to be stringent, since the offspring is non-kosher, and actually we still require that its conception be from a kosher animal? The verse states “seh kesavim”: in any case, since its mother is a ewe, even though its father is not a ram.
gershom:a6.1: He calls it non-kosher, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: that is, since it teaches in this language, “And which is this? This is a non-kosher animal born from a kosher one,” and does not teach “this is what emerges from a kosher one,” learn from it that it speaks according to Rabbi Shimon, for whom it is fully non-kosher. And it says, “but you may eat [what comes] with one sign,” that is, a partial sign. Learn from it that he does not require its head and the majority of its body.
gershom:a7.1: This tanna holds like him on one: that a non-kosher animal born from a kosher one is non-kosher.
gershom:a8.1: And disagrees with him on one: for Rabbi Shimon holds that it is not permitted for consumption unless its head and the majority of its body resemble its mother, as we said with regard to firstborn status, while this tanna holds that even a partial sign permits it for consumption.
gershom:a9.1: And there are those who raise a difficulty: against the baraita, and they object, and from the resolution with which it is resolved, our dilemma is resolved.
gershom:a10.1: Except for Rabbi Eliezer and his disputants: regarding the koy, as it says: What is the koy about which Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis disagree? It is a he-goat that mated with a female gazelle. But the other Rabbis do not say that it becomes pregnant. And it resolves: what is “its conception from a non-kosher animal”? Not truly non-kosher; rather, Rabbi Yirmeya said: it became pregnant from a kalut, whose hooves are not split, the offspring of a cow. And since it calls this kalut non-kosher, saying this is “its conception from a non-kosher animal,” learn from it that it speaks according to Rabbi Shimon, that a non-kosher animal that comes from a kosher one is non-kosher; and it says, “but you may eat what comes with one sign”; learn from it that Rabbi Shimon does not require its head and the majority of its body to resemble its mother. [The Gemara answers:] Actually, he does require it, and this tanna holds like him on one, etc., as we said at first.
gershom:a11.1: Is this to say: that Rabbi Eliezer permits [an offspring whose] conception was from a non-kosher animal because he holds that since its mother is kosher, even though its father is non-kosher, since “this and that cause,” the offspring has in it a kosher cause and is permitted?
gershom:a12.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua holds that “this and that cause” is forbidden: unless its father and its mother are kosher, so that both causes are kosher.
gershom:a13.1: But we have heard them say the opposite, the offspring of a tereifa: even though its father is not a tereifa but kosher and whole.
gershom:a14.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: it may not be sacrificed on the altar. Evidently Rabbi Eliezer holds “this and that cause” is forbidden, and Rabbi Yehoshua holds it is permitted. [The answer:] Actually, in general, as with regard to the altar, Rabbi Eliezer holds “this and that cause” is forbidden; here, with regard to consumption, it is different. If it were so that “this and that cause” is forbidden, let the verse write “ox, kesavim and izzim,” which would imply: until its father and mother are sheep. Why do I need “seh, seh”? Learn from it: a seh in any case, that “this and that cause” is permitted.
gershom:a15.1: The urine of a donkey: what is [the law] regarding drinking it? Water enters, water exits: that is, it drank clear water and passes clear water; therefore they are permitted.
gershom:a16.1: What: shall we say that, since it is turbid, it is squeezed from its body, from its limbs, and is forbidden, like milk, which is squeezed from the body and is forbidden? Or perhaps it is not squeezed [from the body], but water enters, water exits, and that it is turbid is due to its heat, the warmth of the flesh, and it is permitted, since it is not squeezed from its body?
gershom:a17.1: It does not say mittamei: for had it said so, it would imply everything that comes out of a non-kosher animal, whether turbid or not.
gershom:a18.1: Rather, it says min hattamei: that is, these that come out, which are a kind [min] of non-kosher substance, being turbid like a kind of milk, are non-kosher.
rashi:b1.1: And these too: come from a non-kosher animal, for they were inside the non-kosher animal; and even though they are not squeezed from its body, they are forbidden.
rashi:b4.1: That they bring it into their bodies: for they eat from the blossoms of the trees, and from them the honey is made in their innards.
rashi:b4.2: And they do not squeeze it: their honey from their body. This is difficult for Rav Sheshet, for here, since it is not squeezed from their bodies, it is permitted. [Answer:] Rav Sheshet, who said that anything that was inside the non-kosher animal [is forbidden], spoke in accordance with Rabbi Ya’akov, for whom the reason for honey is not that they bring it into their bodies; rather, the Merciful One explicitly permitted it, and it is a decree of the verse.
rashi:b7.1: A non-kosher winged creature: the creature itself; [its prohibition] is written explicitly (Leviticus 11:13): “And these you shall hold in abomination among the birds.”
rashi:b7.2: Rather, a non-kosher winged creature you may not eat: for this is what it is precise to say, “and you may not,” so that you turn and infer from it: but you may eat what a non-kosher winged creature discharges that is not offspring like itself, such as honey. Another version: rather, a non-kosher winged creature you may not eat, and it derives it from the other verse, “All winged swarming creatures,” etc.
rashi:b8.1: Gizzin and wasps: a kind of locust.
rashi:b8.2: Bee honey: they call it simply “honey.” Gizzin honey is called by that [full] name.
rashi:b9.1: Pure: from contracting the impurity of food, since ordinarily it is not [meant] for eating until one intends it [as food].
rashi:b10.1: Pure; evidently it requires intent: [read] as a statement [not a question].
rashi:b10.2: Honey in its hive: and one has not yet intended it [as food], for it is still in its hive. It speaks of bee honey, for only bees have a hive.
rashi:b11.1: Ḥalei of the fallow deer: something like male testicles, which female fallow deer discharge from their womb.
rashi:b11.2: And are forbidden: as a limb from a living animal, since they were torn from the male in the womb.
rashi:b11.3: That pursues the hind: to mate with it.
rashi:b11.4: And they fall out: it pours out much semen, and it congeals.
rashi:b12.1: The skin that emerges opposite the face of a donkey: something like an afterbirth in which the donkey is born.
rashi:b13.1: Pure: from imparting impurity by touch and by carrying.
rashi:b13.2: What, is it not: even when the offspring and the mother are dead, even so the skin does not impart impurity. Evidently he holds that the afterbirth is neither from the offspring nor from the mother, but is merely a secretion.
rashi:b14.1: This is the reading: “No: whether it is alive and its mother alive, or it is dead and its mother alive” [Rashi’s text thus differs from the Davidson English, which reads “alive and its mother dead … dead and its mother alive”]: for it is from the body of the mother, and she is alive. But with regard to consumption, when you assign it to the mother, it is also forbidden.
rashi:b15.1: Mishna. That swallowed: implies that we know for certain that it swallowed it.
rashi:b15.2: Since it is not its growth: rather, it swallowed it alive. But what grows within it is permitted, for what emerges from the kosher is kosher.
rashi:b16.1: Gemara. It spawned it: this kosher fish found inside the non-kosher one was spawned in its body and is its fetus, and it is forbidden.
rashi:b17.1: A non-kosher fish spawns: [it carries] its fetus in its body, like other domesticated and undomesticated animals.
rashi:b17.2: A kosher fish lays eggs: and sits on them and warms them until it brings them out of the shell, like birds.
rashi:b17.3: If so: since a non-kosher fish spawns, [say that] the one it swallowed was digested and became excrement, and this one found inside it, it spawned; it is its fetus, and let it be forbidden.
rashi:b18.1: In the digestive tract [literally, the passage of excrement]: and if it were its fetus, it should be found in the womb.
rashi:b18.2: That he found it whole: its whole form is complete and it is large; and if it were its fetus, it would not stay in the womb that long.
rashi:b19.1: Rav Ashi says: [he understands] the mishna not as where we saw it swallow, but where it was found inside it. And it teaches “that swallowed” because most fish spawn their own species, and this one [would have] spawned another species, so it is as if it swallowed it in our presence.
rashi:b20.1: Any that gives birth: that bears an actual fetus.
rashi:b20.2: Nurses: it has teats; and any that lays eggs has no teats, and it gathers crumbs and sustains its young.
rashi:b20.3: Atalef: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss, calve soriz, “bat.”) It resembles a mouse and has wings.
tosafot:b3.1: You learned it: “that which emerges from the non-kosher is non-kosher.” That [the mishna’s wording] implies it was stated as a sign [an indicator] is no difficulty at all, as we explained above (6a, s.v. lamah).
tosafot:b8.1: Gizzin and wasps: this is our reading, and we do not read “locusts,” for this is a flying creature, like the gizzei dekhalta [mentioned] in Niddah (17a), according to the explanation of Rabbeinu Tam.
tosafot:b12.1: The skin that emerges opposite the face of a donkey: explained as above.
tosafot:b13.1: What, is it not whether it [is dead] and its mother is dead: explanation: evidently the skin is neither from the offspring nor from the mother, but is the seed that hardened [the printed word, nitkadesh, apparently stands for a word meaning “congealed”].
tosafot:b14.1: No: whether it is alive and its mother dead, or it is dead and its mother alive: for the skin comes from between the two of them, from the mother and from the offspring, and therefore it is pure until both of them die. In the Kuntres [Rashi] explained it thus: “whether it and its mother are alive, or it is dead and its mother alive,” [so that] its mother’s being alive is always required. But what we explained seems right, since Rav Ḥisda’s saying “whether it is dead and its mother is dead” implies that his support comes only from our ruling it pure when both are dead; if one of them is alive, there is no support here.
tosafot:b15.1: In brief: Tosafot ask why a non-kosher fish swallowed by a kosher one is forbidden, given the mishna in Oholot (11:7): a dog that ate corpse flesh imparts impurity for three full days, but in birds and fish, only as long as it takes to fall into a fire and be burned; evidently what a fish swallows counts as digested at once, so here too it should be permitted. One cannot distinguish corpse flesh from other foods, since the dog’s three days apply to everything, as Shabbat (155b) explains: the Holy One knows that a dog’s food is scarce, so He keeps its food in its innards three days. One may instead distinguish between prohibition and impurity. Some want to use this mishna to permit a grain of wheat found on Passover inside a chicken; with the distinction between prohibition and impurity, that is no proof. Rabbeinu Tam adds that perhaps one should be stringent like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who requires a full day. And if there is no distinction between prohibition and impurity, our passage must speak of a fish that did not stay long enough to be digested. If so, how can the Gemara say “that one was digested and this one it spawned”? Sometimes it is digested sooner; a fish is not like a dog, whose time is always three days. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b19.1: In brief: The halakha follows Rav Ashi, the latest authority, so one may permit the fish called marenes found inside the fish called blina (Tosafot give the Old French names), even though we did not see it swallow. Nor is our mishna, which permits a kosher fish swallowed by a non-kosher one, a difficulty for Rav Sheshet, who forbids a donkey’s urine, even in the version that forbids that of horses and camels too: the mishna speaks of a kosher fish found inside, and it is obvious that fish go in and fish come out, whereas the water an animal drinks mixes with the moisture of its body. Torat Kohanim teaches about fish: “You shall eat” includes the kosher fish in a non-kosher fish’s innards; might the non-kosher in a kosher one’s innards be included too? The verse says “them.” Why? With animals, what is in a non-kosher animal is non-kosher and what is in a kosher animal is kosher; with fish it is not so, since it is not its growth. That passage gives no proof for forbidding a kosher fish swallowed by a non-kosher one once it has come out: “in the innards of the non-kosher” was said only because of the non-kosher one in the innards of the kosher, and perhaps the case it permits is where it came out, since it is considered digested. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b20.1: A non-kosher fish spawns, a kosher fish lays eggs: in Avoda Zara, chapter Ein Ma’amidin (40a), it explains that both of them lay eggs; this one spawns outside, and that one spawns inside.
gershom:b1.1: And there are those who say that about horses and camels they did not ask, since people do not drink it for any remedy; it is nothing, and is not forbidden, since it is not significant for anything.
gershom:b2.1: When they asked, it was about a donkey, etc. And these too, the urine of a donkey, come from a non-kosher animal and are forbidden. According to this latter version, whether turbid or not, they are forbidden.
gershom:b3.1: That they bring it into their bodies: for they suck it from the plants of the mountains.
gershom:b4.1: And they do not squeeze it from their bodies when they bring it out; rather, as it went in, so it comes out. This is difficult for both versions. For the latter version it is difficult, since this honey comes from a non-kosher creature and is permitted. For the first version it is difficult, since there it said that when they are turbid, even though they are not squeezed from its body, they are forbidden, while here with honey, since they do not squeeze it from their bodies, it is permitted. And Rav Sheshet would tell you: honey is different, for even if it comes from its body it is permitted, since he spoke in accordance with Rabbi Ya’akov, who said that honey, etc.
gershom:b5.1: A non-kosher winged creature: its prohibition is written explicitly. Rather, he derives it from the other verse, as it is written, “these you shall not eat”: a non-kosher winged creature you may not eat, but you may eat what a non-kosher winged creature discharges, bringing it out of its body.
gershom:b7.1: That has no modifier: its name is not attached to that of the forbidden creature; rather, it is called simply “honey,” as it is written, “in the honeycomb” (I Samuel 14:27). Since we say “pure,” evidently it requires intent: for other honey imparts the impurity of food even without intent, and this does not, unless one intended it [as food]. [A note in the printed edition refers here to the Arukh, entry ḥali.] These ḥalei of the fallow deer, which are found in its excrement like eggs: the Sages before Rav Safra thought to say that they are eggs and forbidden for consumption, like a limb from a living animal, since the Torah permitted no eggs except those of birds, [and these resemble] the eggs of an animal that separate from it while it is alive.
gershom:b8.1: Rav Safra said to them: they are not eggs, but the semen of a hart, which goes after the hind to mate with it, and the hind does not accept it because her womb is narrow. When it sees that she does not accept it [a note in the printed edition: in the Arukh the reading is, it goes after the fallow deer, which resembles the hind], and while it pursues her, it carries its semen in its body, and it ripens there a great deal. When it mates with the fallow deer, since the semen has congealed a great deal, it is not absorbed in her body, and she discharges it with her excrement. That semen, since it has ripened, looks like eggs, but it is not eggs, and they are permitted, for they are not like a limb from a living animal.
gershom:b9.1: The skin that emerges opposite the face of a donkey is permitted for consumption: when a donkey is born it has a thin skin over its face, like an afterbirth, but it is not an afterbirth, nor is it attached to its face; rather, it is a creation of its own and merely a secretion.
gershom:b10.1: A baraita supports you: that it is merely a secretion.
gershom:b11.1: The skin that emerges opposite the face of a person: for a person too has a thin skin over his face when he is born, and that skin is neither from the mother nor from the offspring, and it is pure with regard to corpse impurity.
gershom:b12.1: No: whether it is alive and its mother is dead: for we assign it to the living one; otherwise it imparts impurity.
gershom:b13.1: But isn’t it taught: whether it is dead and its mother is dead, it is pure? If it is taught, it is taught.
gershom:b14.1: The reason is that we saw the non-kosher fish swallow the kosher fish: therefore it is permitted for consumption. But if we did not see it swallow, we say it spawned it; that is, the non-kosher fish was pregnant with this kosher fish in its innards.
gershom:b15.1: As it is taught, a non-kosher fish spawns: it becomes pregnant and gives birth to its young.
gershom:b16.1: A kosher fish lays eggs and warms them until they take form, and breaks them open, and they come out.
gershom:b17.1: That one which it swallowed was digested in its innards, and this one found in its innards it spawned; and let it be forbidden.
gershom:b18.1: For example, where he found this kosher fish in the non-kosher one’s digestive tract: for if it had spawned it, it would not be found in the digestive tract but in its afterbirth. Or he found it in the passage of swallowing, where young are not normally found. Or he found it whole: for if it were its young, it would not be fully whole; rather, it certainly swallowed it.
gershom:b19.1: Rav Ashi says: since most non-kosher fish spawn, that is, give birth to, their own kind and not another kind, and this one found in its belly is kosher, it is as if it swallowed it in our presence, for certainly a non-kosher fish spawns only its own kind.
gershom:b20.1: Any that gives birth nurses its young, and any that lays eggs gathers the eggs, sits on them and warms them, and thereby is fruitful and multiplies. And some say “gathers” means that it does not nurse but gathers food in its mouth and throws it before its young, and thereby sustains them.
